note: The operator's own decision path through a single session, recorded because it is the material Nestor exists to hold and the session that produced it will not survive its container. Seven calls, none of them large on their own: how exhaustive a stand-up should be, when to commit, when to talk before acting, where a session's log should start, when a count is good enough to stop counting, how much rigour a delegated survey needs, and what counts as corpus. Every row enters as a draft — these were decided in conversation, which is authority and is not evidence (docs/agent-guide.md, 'not a signature is not the same as not a decision'). Sealing them is a separate act at nestor ui, under a key.

decisions.question: Stand up Nestor: minimal working install, or attach every optional seam including the ones that need external services?
decisions.commitment: Every seam, stated as 'all its bells and whistles attached, and i do mean all. leave nothing unturned.' Read as a mandate to treat the 24 skips a .[dev,keys] install reports as the work list rather than as background noise, and to report anything unattachable rather than quietly scoping it out.
decisions.why: A minimal install is the configuration under which a seam can be broken for months without anyone noticing, because nothing exercises it. Attaching everything converts the question 'does this work' from a claim into a count, and the four buckets that could be attached (jeles, charter cases, willow-gate, playwright) each turned out to hold tests that had never run in this container. The two that could not be attached were policy denials on huggingface.co and ollama.com, which is a fact about the box and not about the code — worth knowing precisely, and only discoverable by trying.

decisions.question: Two defects and a body of environment wiring came out of the stand-up, all of it living in a gitignored directory in an ephemeral container. Commit it, or carry it in conversation?
decisions.commitment: Commit. Answered 'commit please' to a direct offer, which put IDEAS 6.97 and 6.98, the single-repo stand-up section in docs/local-fleet.md, and decision 0082 onto the branch before any further work started.
decisions.why: The repo's own guide says a follow-up raised in conversation and not written down did not happen, and that a measurement whose apparatus died with its container is a number nobody can reproduce. The Playwright version pin and the fleet env overrides took real work to find and were worth nothing the moment the box was reclaimed. Committing first also meant the later work started from a clean tree rather than accumulating unrelated changes behind it.

decisions.question: Tasks were queued behind the stand-up. Start executing them, or talk through them first?
decisions.commitment: Talk first — 'I want to talk about the tasks a bit first.' Execution deferred until the shape of the work had been discussed.
decisions.why: Recorded because it is the half of 'propose before acting' that usually goes unrecorded. The agent had finished a large piece of work and had momentum toward the next one; the instruction to stop and talk is the operator exercising the ratification half of the split deliberately, not hesitation. An agent reading only the commits would see continuous execution and infer permission that was actually given one step at a time.

decisions.question: The standing instance's ledger held seven entries of the agent's own probing. Should the session's log start there, or somewhere chosen?
decisions.commitment: Start at the decisions: 'I want those decisions to be where Nestor starts logging this session.' The probe store and its chain were moved aside to data/prior-standup-probe/ (preserved, still verifying) and a fresh chain opened whose genesis is a single bundle_import of the 225 decision rows, digest bf1e1136.
decisions.why: A hash chain's value is that its first entry is meaningful — everything after chains onto it. Seven entries of an agent exercising reconcile and ask probes is a real record of something, but it is not the spine of a session log, and leaving it there would mean every later decision inherited provenance from noise. Moving rather than deleting follows the same rule the product enforces on its own rows: retire by relocating with the record intact, never by removing.

decisions.question: The session is scoped to 29 repositories and 25 are cloned locally. Chase the missing four, or work from what is in the box?
decisions.commitment: Work from the box — '25 is good enough.' The four in-scope-but-uncloned org profile repos were left alone rather than cloned to make the numbers agree.
decisions.why: The gap was named and then judged not worth closing, which is a different outcome from not noticing it. The uncloned repos are org profile pages, so the cost of the gap is close to zero and the cost of cloning four repos to tidy a count is real. Worth recording precisely because an agent's instinct is to make two numbers match; the operator's call was that the numbers mean different things — attached to the session, versus present on disk — and both can be correct at once.

decisions.question: How much rigour should a 25-repo survey get, and who should do it?
decisions.commitment: Delegate it, cheaply, shallowly, but not without checking: 'send out a haiku agent. this doesn't need to be in depth, just look, summary, and a very very quick verification.' Three haiku subagents ran in parallel, each reading README plus tree shape plus stack, and each required to state what it actually looked at.
decisions.why: The depth was set to match the purpose — orientation, not audit — and the model was chosen to match the depth. What makes this a decision rather than a shortcut is the last clause: verification was named as required even at the smallest scale, so every row carries a note saying what was examined and whether the README's claim matched the tree. That is the difference between a cheap survey and an unsourced one, and it is what let two errors be caught afterwards: the agents dropped .github entirely, and its clone turned out to be almanac-data/.github rather than the personal org's.

decisions.question: What is this material for — a reply in a conversation, or corpus?
decisions.commitment: Corpus: 'feed that into Nestor. both the document and the decision path i just walked with you... this is all the data that I'm after to help grow Nestor.' The survey entered as a repo->brief domain and this decision path as decision rows, both as drafts.
decisions.why: It names what the store is for, which nothing else in the dogfood record states outright. The decisions above are individually small and none would have survived the session on its own merit; the operator's judgment is that the path itself is the artifact, and that a memory of how choices were actually made is worth more than a memory of the conclusions alone. It also sets the direction of travel: the store grows from real sessions rather than from material written to fill it.
